policy: Original educational items. Every A-D alternative receives an authored rationale. A section citation and URL are source evidence, not a legally binding review stamp; do not label frozen until final current-source/effective-date check.

items.primary_law: 21 U.S.C. §351(d)(2); 21 U.S.C. §352(a)(1) may additionally apply if labeling is false
items.new_decisive_difference: Substitution under §351(d)(2), distinct from previously tested assay failure/false label.

A.rationale: Correct. Substituting another substance wholly or in part is an independent adulteration ground under FD&C Act section 501(d)(2).

B.rationale: Incorrect. The presented defect is the substituted substance, not how prominently required labeling appears.

C.rationale: Incorrect. The scenario does not identify a missing manufacturer address.

D.rationale: Incorrect. No poisonous container is described, although the product itself has an adulteration defect.

items.new_decisive_difference: Poisonous or deleterious container under §351(a)(3), not contamination from insanitary storage.

A.rationale: Correct. A poisonous or deleterious drug container capable of rendering contents injurious meets section 501(a)(3).

B.rationale: Incorrect. 21 U.S.C. §351(a)(3) addresses potentially injurious containers independent of an assay of contents.

C.rationale: Correct. Container-related adulteration is a separate fact from tested tablet strength or purity.

D.rationale: Incorrect. Statutory adulteration does not require a previously announced recall.

items.new_decisive_difference: Lack of conspicuous required warning under §352(c), distinct from false therapeutic claim under §352(a).

A.rationale: Incorrect. There is no competing branded imitation in the facts.

B.rationale: Incorrect. No ingredient substitution is described.

C.rationale: Correct. Section 502(c), 21 U.S.C. §352(c), addresses conspicuous placement and ordinary readability.

D.rationale: Incorrect. Typography is not evidence of a poisonous container.

items.new_decisive_difference: Misleading container under §352(i)(1) despite accurate printed count.

A.rationale: Incorrect. Misleading retail presentation is not, by itself, a controlled inventory discrepancy.

B.rationale: Incorrect. A truthful count does not eliminate the distinct prohibition on a misleading container.

C.rationale: Incorrect. Misleading packaging can be misbranding without an assay failure.

D.rationale: Correct. 21 U.S.C. §352(i)(1) independently treats a misleading container as misbranding.

items.new_decisive_difference: Package identifier investigation sampling rule 3 or 10%, not only suspect-product quarantine.

A.rationale: Incorrect. When ten percent of the suspect packages exceeds three, the higher count applies.

B.rationale: Correct. Section 582(d)(4)(A)(ii)(II) requires at least three packages or 10%, whichever is greater.

C.rationale: Incorrect. The statutory sample requirement is not simply one item per manufacturer.

D.rationale: Incorrect. The cited investigation sampling provision specifies a threshold of at least three or ten percent, whichever is greater.

items.new_decisive_difference: Six-year retention after ILLEGITIMATE disposition, not the previously tested suspect investigation clock.

A.rationale: Correct. 21 U.S.C. §360eee-1(d)(4)(B)(v) uses the end of disposition as the retention clock for those records.

B.rationale: Incorrect. Two business days concerns certain official requests for tracing records, not the disposition-retention period.

C.rationale: Incorrect. The disposition record requirement does not end on the pharmacy inventory date.

D.rationale: Incorrect. Neither the duration nor the starting point matches the specific federal rule.

items.new_decisive_difference: Official records request under §582(d)(1)(D) two-business-day clock, rather than outsourced storage authorization.

A.rationale: Correct. Section 582(d)(1)(D) sets a two-business-day deadline unless an alternate reasonable time is determined based on the request.

B.rationale: Incorrect. The statutory clock for a qualifying official request is much shorter.

C.rationale: Incorrect. A recordkeeping service does not release the dispenser from its statutory obligations.

D.rationale: Correct. An appropriate official can request the transaction information, statement and history received from the prior owner.

items.new_decisive_difference: Licensed healthcare practitioner exception §582(d)(5), rather than small-company headcount exemption.

A.rationale: Incorrect. Section 582(d)(5) expressly treats covered practitioners separately in the ordinary course of professional practice.

B.rationale: Incorrect. The statute exempts certain DSCSA subsections, not adulteration, misbranding, or quality requirements.

C.rationale: Correct. The statute excepts eligible licensed practitioners and supervised licensed individuals from subsections (d)(1) and (d)(4).

D.rationale: Incorrect. Routine lawful practitioner administration is not automatically wholesale distribution.

items.primary_law: 21 U.S.C. §360bbb-3(a)(2)-(3); FDA current Paxlovid approval/EUA entries (November 2026)
items.new_decisive_difference: Actual Paxlovid adult approved vs pediatric EUA indication, not ordinary prescription schedule classification.

A.rationale: Incorrect. The authorized pediatric use is under the separate EUA, not the adult approved indication.

B.rationale: Incorrect. FDA has approved a specified adult COVID-19 use.

C.rationale: Incorrect. The authorized pediatric population has specified age, weight and risk criteria.

D.rationale: Correct. FDA approval for qualifying adults and EUA for specified pediatric patients coexist.

items.effective_date_watch: FDA EUA pediatric and adult approval statuses may change by exam date

items.primary_law: 21 U.S.C. §360bbb-3; FDA Gohibic authorized use, April 2026 amendment
items.new_decisive_difference: Gohibic hospitalized adult IMV/ECMO 48-hour EUA, not practitioner training or residency hours.

A.rationale: Incorrect. The cited FDA COVID-19 pathway is an EUA, not general approval without a time condition.

B.rationale: Incorrect. The EUA imposes a timing window beyond patient age and hospitalization.

C.rationale: Correct. FDA lists Gohibic EUA use for hospitalized adults when initiated within 48 hours of starting IMV or ECMO.

D.rationale: Incorrect. The clock refers to the patient's start of invasive mechanical ventilation or ECMO.

items.effective_date_watch: Gohibic EUA scope and effective authorization may change by exam date

items.primary_law: FDA Emergency Use Authorizations for Drugs and Non-Vaccine Biological Products (termination notice); 21 U.S.C. §360bbb-3(b),(g)
items.new_decisive_difference: FDA future-effective EUA termination, not renewal/report deadline mathematics.

A.rationale: Correct. The declaration termination was announced in 2026 but applies to listed COVID-drug/biologic EUAs beginning June 29, 2027, absent intervening changes.

B.rationale: Incorrect. The planned termination takes effect in June 2027, not on the announcement date.

C.rationale: Incorrect. The FDA notice specifies a termination effective date and does not require a fresh extension to cover the time before it.

D.rationale: Incorrect. EUA termination does not automatically rescind independent NDA/BLA approvals.

items.effective_date_watch: June 29, 2027 scheduled termination; reverify before publication and exam

items.primary_law: 21 U.S.C. §360bbb-3(e)(1)(A)(ii)(I)-(III); active authorization-specific healthcare provider/patient fact sheet
items.new_decisive_difference: EUA patient authorization/risk/refusal disclosures, not HIPAA/Part 2 consent.

A.rationale: Incorrect. Emergency authorization is a separate status and is not ordinary marketing approval.

B.rationale: Correct. Section 564(e)(1)(A)(ii) calls for informing individuals of emergency authorization, known and potential benefits/risks and uncertainties.

C.rationale: Correct. 21 U.S.C. §360bbb-3(e)(1)(A)(ii)(III) describes recipients' informed choice and alternatives.

D.rationale: Incorrect. Emergency authorization necessarily includes potential risks and uncertainties; no such guarantee exists.

items.effective_date_watch: Specific EUA letter and fact-sheet requirements must be checked if a real product is later inserted

items.primary_law: 21 U.S.C. §§355(a), 381; FDA import requirements for FDA-approved human drugs
items.new_decisive_difference: Foreign-manufactured same-ingredient drug outside U.S. application, not compounding copies of approved drugs.

A.rationale: Incorrect. The U.S. approval extends to an approved application and its authorized manufacturing and labeling conditions.

B.rationale: Correct. FDA notes foreign-made versions not manufactured pursuant to a U.S. approval may be unapproved new drugs.

C.rationale: Incorrect. Foreign manufacture can be lawful when it follows applicable FDA approvals, establishment requirements and import rules.

D.rationale: Incorrect. A prescription does not create an NDA/ANDA approval or legal importation authorization.

items.primary_law: 21 U.S.C. §§355(a),381; FDA Personal Importation policy (personal use vs resale)
items.new_decisive_difference: FDA personal import discretionary policy vs bulk pharmacy resale, not controlled product ID or prescription.

A.rationale: Incorrect. The legality of marketing/importing a drug is separate from a patient's prescription.

B.rationale: Incorrect. FDA's personal-importation considerations do not exempt wholesale commercial stocking.

C.rationale: Correct. FDA defines personal importation as not for further sale or distribution; enforcement discretion is not a retail import license.

D.rationale: Correct. Commercial pharmacy importation is not the same as a possible case-by-case FDA enforcement decision for an individual.

items.primary_law: FD&C Act §503A(b)(1)(A)(i), 21 U.S.C. §353a(b)(1)(A)(i); FDA 503A bulk drug substances
items.new_decisive_difference: Ingredient meets monograph and registration pathway but lacks COA; opposite deficiency from E30-187's nonqualifying API with COA.

A.rationale: Incorrect. Eligible patient-specific 503A preparations may qualify for statutory exemptions from new drug approval, subject to 503A conditions.

B.rationale: Incorrect. Drug scheduling does not supply the missing 503A documentation condition.

C.rationale: Incorrect. FDA registration and applicable quality requirements matter, not a blanket foreign-source requirement.

D.rationale: Correct. Section 503A bulk-substance conditions require a valid COA in addition to eligibility and manufacturing-establishment registration.

items.effective_date_watch: 503A COA plus FDA-registered manufacturer; watch FDA policy changes

items.primary_law: 21 U.S.C. §381(a); FDA import requirements for FDA-approved human drug products
items.new_decisive_difference: Import Customs entry notice and bond for otherwise FDA-approved drug, not DSCSA receipt of domestic inventory.

A.rationale: Incorrect. State pharmacy licensure does not replace federal customs import-entry procedures.

B.rationale: Incorrect. Facility registration and lawful product approval do not remove import entry reporting requirements.

C.rationale: Correct. FDA describes notice of entry and entry bond under customs procedures while FDA reviews admissibility of imported regulated goods.

D.rationale: Incorrect. This is commercial importation rather than a noncommercial personal import.

items.primary_law: NIOSH List of Hazardous Drugs in Healthcare Settings, 2024; 29 CFR 1910.1200; applicable Massachusetts Board rules
items.new_decisive_difference: NIOSH hazard identification vs federal DEA scheduling and enforceable OSHA standard, not USP 800 assessment of risk.

A.rationale: Incorrect. The OSHA standard depends on the chemical hazard and workplace exposure facts, not solely a NIOSH listing.

B.rationale: Correct. The NIOSH list is a worker-exposure identification resource, not the federal Controlled Substances Act scheduling table.

C.rationale: Correct. 29 CFR 1910.1200 can require employer communication, safety information, and employee training.

D.rationale: Correct. A drug's FDA marketing status does not independently decide whether covered hazardous chemicals and foreseeable workplace exposures trigger OSHA's HCS.

items.effective_date_watch: NIOSH 2024 list reference vs OSHA regulations

items.primary_law: 29 CFR 1910.1200(b)(6)(vii); OSHA Hospital Pharmacy HCS eTool
items.new_decisive_difference: OSHA HCS finished-solid-form exemption, not USP 800 containment category.

A.rationale: Correct. 29 CFR 1910.1200(b)(6)(vii) excepts a covered drug in solid final form for direct patient administration; other rules may still govern it.

B.rationale: Incorrect. Open powder handling is not an intact solid finished tablet for direct patient administration.

C.rationale: Incorrect. OSHA explains that tablets intended for employee crushing before administration are not in final form under this exemption.

D.rationale: Incorrect. A liquid requiring manipulation is outside the stated solid-final-form exemption.

items.effective_date_watch: HCS final-form exception requires facts about intended employee manipulation; do not import USP800 exception

items.primary_law: 29 CFR 1910.1200(b)(5)(iii), (g),(h); OSHA Hospital Pharmacy Hazard Communication Standard eTool
items.new_decisive_difference: FDA label exception to OSHA HCS labels, not patient prescription label details.

A.rationale: Incorrect. OSHA's FDA-drug-labeling exception is not a blanket exemption from all workplace hazard communication duties.

B.rationale: Correct. 29 CFR 1910.1200(b)(5)(iii) addresses HCS labeling; other criteria-based duties still apply.

C.rationale: Incorrect. The OSHA exception depends on FDA labeling requirements, not the fact of repackaging.

D.rationale: Incorrect. FDA-labeling treatment does not itself remove applicable SDS requirements.

items.effective_date_watch: FDA labeling only exception not an HCS SDS/training exemption

items.primary_law: 29 CFR 1910.1200(h)(1)-(3); OSHA hazardous drug exposure guidance
items.new_decisive_difference: Worker training for foreseeable exposure/new hazardous drug including housekeeping, not response to an already occurred spill.

A.rationale: Correct. Section 1910.1200(h)(1) applies at initial assignment and when a new chemical hazard not previously covered is introduced.

B.rationale: Incorrect. OSHA's covered exposure provisions include relevant support staff and housekeepers.

C.rationale: Incorrect. Foreseeable emergency exposure is part of the standard; proactive training and information are required.

D.rationale: Correct. Section 1910.1200(h)(2)-(3) requires effective information and training about hazards and protections.
